text: A carnival performer with no gift for danger straps on the bells of a court jester and walks into a palace held by a usurper. The disguise is the engine: for a hundred and one minutes everything depends on a man who cannot fight, cannot plot and cannot stop talking being mistaken for someone who can do all three. Norman Panama keeps interrupting the swordplay to sing and the songs to push a joke six turns past the point where jokes usually die, and the patter is structure rather than decoration - comedy built like choreography, rhythm doing the work that stunts do elsewhere. Behind it sits a stolen English throne, taken exactly as seriously as it needs to be. The National Film Registry keeps a copy, which is a solemn fate for a picture this content to be silly.

The romance and the ruin are the same scenes: the man courting her is also the man handing her the glass. Blake Edwards takes 117 black-and-white minutes over it, and the offices and apartments of 1962 stay respectable-looking long after the two people inside them have begun arranging their days around a bottle. The dread comes from housekeeping detail rather than incident - a drawer, a hidden pint, a morning explained away before anyone has asked. There is no villain here to blame. Two people like each other and like drinking, and the film is patient enough to show how long that combination can pass for happiness. He is charming while he lies; she believes him because the lies are small and the affection is not. Nothing in the first hour announces itself as a warning.

The voice that carries a chorus is often not the voice on the record sleeve. Morgan Neville spends 89 minutes with backup singers - the people whose harmonies are inseparable from records by the biggest bands in popular music, and whose names were not printed on them. The interest is less in injustice than in craft: what it takes to blend, to sit under another singer's line, to be indispensable and anonymous in the same breath. Proximity is the subject. These are performers who stood a few paces from the front of the stage for whole careers, near enough to know exactly what that position was made of, and the film lets them describe it in their own terms rather than through the stars they served. The Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature handed them, for a season, the microphone at the centre.

The detective and the victim are the same man, and the case is still in progress inside his own body. Frank Bigelow, an accountant, has been given a poison with no remedy and roughly a day left to spend, so he spends it retracing his own recent movements toward whoever chose him. Rudolph Maté holds the whole thing to 83 minutes, which is less a stylistic choice than an obligation: the clock in the story and the clock on the projector are running the same errand. It also changes the genre's arithmetic. A man in Bigelow's position cannot be threatened, bought or warned off, so the usual obstacles fall away and what remains is motion - offices, hotel corridors, and a chain of crooked businessmen who never expected anyone to come asking in this particular condition.

A Northern industrialist wants his mills built close to the cotton, and one family in a Southern town means to be the partner he picks. What follows is largely a conversation about percentages. William Wyler gives that negotiation the weight other pictures give to gunfire, because inside this house the two amount to the same thing: the relatives need one another's money, nobody trusts anybody, and every courtesy at the table is a position being held. The year is 1900, and what the town can offer Chicago is land and hands, priced low; the family's ambition and the region's condition are one transaction seen from either end. An Academy Award for Best Actress came out of it, and the reason is legible in the pacing - the person who never raises her voice is the one arranging the room.

The house is a place of business, and a child has grown up inside it knowing no other arrangement. Pretty Baby puts that in New Orleans in 1917 and refuses to editorialize, which is what makes it hard to sit with. Louis Malle treats the brothel as a household first - routines, rivalries, dull afternoons, work going on down the hall - and lets a twelve-year-old move through rooms whose function she takes to be ordinary. The camera keeps a level, unhurried distance, neither leering nor scolding, so judgment has to be supplied from outside the frame. Period songs carry most of the atmosphere, and the song score took an Academy Award. Very little is explained, and nothing is arranged to make the arrangement bearable.

Kate loves a journalist with no money and lives on the goodwill of an aunt who would cut her off for it. Then a terminally ill American heiress arrives in Europe, wealthy, traveling and glad of company, and Kate begins arranging introductions. The plan is never spoken in full; that is also the film's method. Iain Softley shoots the drawing rooms and hotels in low, crowded light where faces are only half available, and the clothes carry the economics - everything Kate wears was bought with the money she is trying not to lose. The Academy Award for Best Cinematography went to that withholding. The question is not whether the scheme is wicked, since it plainly is, but how reasonable it looks from inside a life with one exit, and how little time the heiress has to waste on being deceived.

Four riders, a mountain trail, and a reward that will not divide evenly. A bounty hunter takes his man and immediately loses control of the situation, because the two strangers who helped him now consider themselves partners, and the prisoner has worked out that talk is the only weapon left to him. Anthony Mann keeps it to 91 minutes and to open country, where nobody can be put anywhere: every conversation happens within earshot, and the party has to sleep in the same clearing as the man it is escorting. Westerns usually take their tension from what is over the ridge. This one takes it from the arithmetic of shares, and from the fact that the captive is the shrewdest judge of character in the group. The screenplay won an Academy Award; the plot is a few people talking one another into betrayal, one conversation at a time.

Thomas tells stories constantly, and nobody on the reservation wants to hear them. Victor barely speaks, and he needs money to travel and collect the remains of the father who walked out ten years ago; Thomas has the money, on the condition that he comes along. That is the film: two young men, 89 minutes, a long trip and no way to avoid each other's company. What binds them is older than the trip. Thomas's parents died in a fire in 1976 and Victor's father carried Thomas out of it, which leaves one of them permanently grateful to a man the other cannot forgive. Chris Eyre plays a great deal of this as comedy, dry and needling, delivered through the oversize glasses and unstoppable narration of a boy nobody listens to. The Sundance audience gave it their award, and the humor is a large part of why.

A cowboy comes down from Montana to a Phoenix rodeo, decides within a day that a cafe singer named Cherie will be his wife, and cannot conceive that this requires her agreement. The film is stranger than its billing as a romantic comedy. Beauregard Decker courts the way he works stock - with confidence, force and no malice at all - while Cherie, who is saving for Hollywood and has been handled before, spends the picture trying to reach a place where nobody knows her name. Joshua Logan lets that discomfort stand instead of smoothing it into charm. Then the weather closes the road and the bus puts everyone down in one small room, with nothing to do but look at what has been going on. Virgil Blessing, the older cowboy riding with Decker, has seen it from the start and says almost nothing.

Almost nothing happens except conversation, and the conversation is about Fourier, social mobility and the rules of a very small world. Whit Stillman gathers a set of young New Yorkers in a Manhattan apartment where they play bridge until dawn and treat social mobility with the seriousness of people reviewing a diagnosis. A student with radical politics and less money joins them, and rather than resisting him they adopt him, find his criticisms genuinely interesting, and ask for more - which is funnier and sadder than hostility would have been. Ninety-nine minutes, most of them after midnight, most of them in evening clothes. The film takes these people at their own estimate and lets the distance between that estimate and the world supply the comedy. Its screenplay won an Academy Award; every laugh in it is a matter of syntax.

Frankie Machine leaves prison sober, carrying an old drum set and an intention to make a living with it. The neighborhood he comes back to has other plans: the card game he used to deal for wants his hands again, his old supplier has not moved, and the rooms he returns to are the same rooms. Otto Preminger spends 119 minutes on the narrowing of options, which is the honest shape for this material - not a plunge but a sequence of doors held open by people being friendly. The drum kit is the entire hope of the picture, and it is heavy. Honest work means playing for someone who is listening, and playing requires steady hands. The score took an Academy Award and behaves less like accompaniment than like a symptom, pushing the tempo whenever Frankie's own is about to give.

Painting is difficult to film: the work is silent, static and mostly done alone. Vincente Minnelli's answer is to put the color of the canvases into everything around them, so that fields, skies and plain rooms arrive already composed, and the Academy Award for Best Art Direction in color reads as a description of the method rather than a decoration on it. The rest is a story about dependency. Vincent is kept going by his brother Theo's money, and every stretch of work is underwritten by another man's patience; when Paul Gauguin turns up, two painters with incompatible tempers try to work in the same proximity. Across 122 minutes the film declines to treat the illness as the source of the talent. It treats it as the thing that keeps interrupting the work.

Two ships, two commanders, and a stretch of ocean neither can see through. An American destroyer escort picks up a German submarine, and the film becomes an exchange of guesses: each captain building a model of the other's thinking, acting on it, then waiting to see what comes back. Nearly everything is instruments and inference - a bearing, a delay, a decision to hold silence one minute longer - and Dick Powell cuts between the two vessels so that both halves of every guess are visible while the crews themselves know nothing. The result is a war picture with almost no visible enemy and considerable respect for one. It runs 97 minutes, most of them in hot compartments where men wait on someone else's arithmetic. The Academy Award for Best Special Effects covers the water; the tension is in the pauses.
